title: Energy After the Shock
gist: This is an FP Live event listing rather than a full article: it promotes a July 29, 2026 interview with energy historian Daniel Yergin. Its substantive content is a compact bull-case framing for crude — the Strait of Hormuz is shut again, the Houthis are attempting to block Saudi exports through the Red Sea, global crude reservoirs have not been restored, and China may drop its export curbs — plus deks from adjacent FP analyses arguing the oil market is more vulnerable than Trump believes and that Iran has time on its side.

insights.claim: Oil prices are rising again with the Strait of Hormuz once again shut down and the Houthis attempting to block Saudi exports through the Red Sea, and this time they may not come down so quickly.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Two simultaneous chokepoint disruptions argue for a persistent rather than transient crude premium; size energy exposure for duration.
insights.quote: Oil prices are once again on the rise—and this time, they may not come down so quickly.
insights.locator: Oil prices are once again on the rise

insights.claim: Global reservoirs of crude have not been restored after earlier drawdowns, which removes the buffer that dampened previous price spikes.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Depleted inventories mean any incremental supply loss transmits straight to price — the key asymmetry versus the 2022 analogue.
insights.quote: global reservoirs of crude haven’t been restored
insights.locator: Oil prices are once again on the rise

insights.claim: China may drop its export curbs, adding a further upward impulse to crude prices alongside the Hormuz and Red Sea disruptions.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: A Chinese policy shift is the least-priced of the three catalysts listed — watch Beijing's export quota announcements.
insights.quote: and China may drop its export curbs
insights.locator: Oil prices are once again on the rise

insights.claim: Foreign Policy's framing is that depleted reserves and changed circumstances make oil price spikes more likely this time than Trump believes, per its analysis by Ali Ahmadi titled 'The Oil Market Is Much More Vulnerable Than Trump Believes.'
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: An explicit against-the-White-House view on oil vulnerability; useful as a contrarian marker versus official reassurance.
insights.quote: Depleted reserves and changed circumstances make price spikes more likely this time around.
insights.locator: The Oil Market Is Much More Vulnerable Than Trump Believes

insights.claim: Keith Johnson's accompanying FP analysis frames the Iran standoff as one in which the clock is ticking for global oil markets while Iran has the time, implying Tehran gains from delay.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Asymmetric time preference favors Iran, arguing against betting on a quick de-escalation trade in energy.
insights.quote: The clock is ticking for global oil markets, and Iran has the time.
insights.locator: Trump's Epic Fury Can't Resolve His Iran Quagmire

themes.theme: Structural questions beyond the price spike

insights.claim: The strategic question posed is not the immediate price shock but how countries and companies adapt behavior longer term — what the crisis means for key chokepoints, trading relationships, and how economies explore renewables.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Second-order effects — rerouted trade and accelerated renewables capex — are where multi-year positioning sits, not the spot price.
insights.quote: Beyond the immediate price shock, how will countries and companies adapt their behavior in the longer term?

insights.claim: Robert A. Manning's companion FP analysis argues the closure of Hormuz signals the slow death of the global commons and is a sign of worse things to come.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: If chokepoint contestation generalizes, shipping insurance, naval-adjacent defense and inventory-heavy supply chains reprice structurally.
insights.quote: Hormuz is a sign of worse things to come.
insights.locator: The Slow Death of the Global Commons

insights.claim: The analyst FP has selected to interpret the shock is Daniel Yergin, vice chairman of S&P Global and chairman of CERAWeek, author of The Prize and The New Map.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Yergin's S&P Global platform makes his read a proxy for institutional energy-consensus formation; the July 29 session is worth monitoring.

insights.claim: Nate Swanson, a career State Department official who served most recently as an Iran negotiator and was subsequently outside government, accurately predicted how Iran would respond to U.S. strikes and how it might overplay its hand after signing the memorandum of understanding.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Identifies a forecaster with a demonstrated track record on Iranian escalation behavior — a source worth tracking over institutional consensus.
insights.quote: he accurately predicted how Iran would respond to U.S. strikes and how it might overplay its hand after signing the memorandum of understanding
insights.locator: Where the Iran Conflict Goes From Here

insights.claim: The United States ousted Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro in January and took out Iran's senior leadership in February, then turned to Cuba, where after five months of a U.S. oil blockade Havana is restructuring its economy and publicly welcoming diplomacy with Washington.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: A three-country pattern of U.S. coercive regime pressure inside seven months — a template for handicapping the next target and its energy implications.
insights.quote: After the United States ousted Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro in January and took out Iran’s senior leadership in February, U.S. President Donald Trump set his sights on Cuba

insights.claim: Ukraine's long-range drones have brought the war home to Russians to a degree Putin has recently acknowledged, giving Kyiv battlefield momentum to argue at the NATO summit in Ankara.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Russian domestic exposure to drone strikes is the variable most likely to move peace-talk odds — watch refinery and infrastructure hit rates.
